l: Dorians, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The Dorians assigned Argos to Temenus and allowed Cresphontes to obtain Messenia by lot. The older Messenians remained in the country and agreed to Cresphontes as king and to a division of the land among the Dorians.

l: Heraclidæ, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The return of the Heraclidæ, together with the expedition of the Dorians, drove the descendants of Neleus from Messenia two generations after the war against Ilium. The descendants of Æpytus later became known as Æpytidæ instead of Heraclidæ.

l: Cresphontes, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Cresphontes obtained Messenia through a rigged-looking lot when the clay lot of the sons of Aristodemus dissolved in water. He made Stenyclerus his royal residence, but wealthy opponents killed him and all his sons except Æpytus.

l: Æpytus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Æpytus, the youngest son of Cresphontes, survived the murder of his family after being raised by Cypselus. The Arcadians and other Dorian rulers restored him to Messenia, where he punished the murderers and won support through gifts and favorable treatment.

l: Stenyclerus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Stenyclerus became the royal residence under Cresphontes, replacing the earlier centers at Andania, Arene, and Pylos. Cresphontes built his palace there for himself and his sons.

l: Artemis Limnas, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The temple of Artemis Limnas stood on the border of Messenia and was shared by the Messenians and Lacedæmonians as the only Dorians with a share there. Conflicting traditions about an incident at the temple involving maidens, Teleclus, and Messenians became part of the causes alleged for the later war.

l: Teleclus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Teleclus was the Lacedæmonian king who, according to the Lacedæmonian account, was killed while trying to prevent the violation of Lacedæmonian maidens at Artemis Limnas. The Messenian account instead says that he plotted against prominent Messenians by disguising armed Spartan youths as maidens, and was killed with them.

l: Alcamenes, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Alcamenes, the son of Teleclus, was king at Lacedæmon during a later generation of conflict. He was appointed general for the night attack that captured Amphea.

l: Antiochus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Antiochus, one of the sons of Phintas, was king of Messenia alongside his brother Androcles. He opposed surrendering Polychares, argued for submitting the case to arbitration, and became sole king after Androcles was killed; he later died before the war began openly.

l: Androcles, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Androcles, son of Phintas and fellow king of Messenia, argued that Polychares should be surrendered because of his violent conduct. His dispute with Antiochus led to armed conflict between their supporters, and Antiochus’ party killed him and his leading partisans.

l: Polychares, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Polychares was a Messenian victor at Olympia who entrusted his cattle to Euæphnus for grazing. After Euæphnus sold the cattle and killed Polychares’ son, Polychares sought justice in Lacedæmon but, receiving no redress, became enraged and attempted to kill every Lacedæmonian he encountered.

l: Euæphnus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Euæphnus was a Spartan entrusted by Polychares with cattle but sold them to merchants and falsely claimed that pirates had taken them. After being exposed, he lured and killed Polychares’ son, becoming the central figure in the dispute over whether Polychares should be surrendered.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Sparta received a Messenian appeal for justice against Euæphnus but did not provide redress. Its authorities later received conflicting proposals concerning Polychares and secretly prepared for war rather than accepting arbitration.

l: Euphaes, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Euphaes succeeded his father Antiochus as king of Messenia. During his reign, the Lacedæmonians launched their first attack by capturing Amphea.

l: Amphea, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Amphea was a small Messenian town near Laconia, situated on a high, well-watered hill and useful as a base for war. The Lacedæmonians captured it in a night attack while its gates were open and killed the Messenians they found there, including suppliants at temples and altars.

l: first Messenian War, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The First Messenian War began with the Lacedæmonian night attack on Amphea during the reign of Euphaes. The Lacedæmonians had sworn to continue the war despite its length or reverses until they had won Messenia.

l: capture of Amphea, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The capture of Amphea was the first attack made by the Lacedæmonians against Messenia. It occurred in the second year of the ninth Olympiad, under the command of Alcamenes, after the town was found without a garrison.

l: Messenian–Lacedæmonian conflict, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The conflict arose from competing traditions about the death of Teleclus, the treatment of Polychares and Euæphnus, and earlier disputes involving Cresphontes and the division of territory. The Lacedæmonians rejected arbitration and ultimately began open hostilities with the capture of Amphea.

l: mysteries of the Great Goddesses, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The mysteries of the Great Goddesses were brought from Eleusis to Messenia by Caucon and later reformed or taught by Lycus and Methapus. They were associated with Andania, where they continued to be celebrated, and Sybotas required annual rites before them.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit introduces the Messenian war and explains that Aristomenes will be discussed later, while comparing the accounts of Myron of Priene and Rhianus of Bene. After the capture of Amphea, the Messenians prepare for war under Euphaes, fight the Lacedæmonians in two major battles, and withdraw to Ithome after suffering financial losses, desertions, and pestilence. A Delphic oracle requires the sacrifice of a pure virgin from the family of the Æpytidæ, leading to the death of Aristodemus’s daughter and a disputed interpretation of the oracle. Euphaes dies after the second battle, and Aristodemus is elected king as the war continues with raids and support from Arcadian allies.

l: Messenian War, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The war is called the Messenian war because of the disasters that befell the Messenians, rather than because of the attacking force. Myron describes events from the capture of Amphea to the death of Aristodemus, while Rhianus begins with events after the battle at the great trench.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aristomenes is presented as the Messenian hero who first brought honour to the name of Messene. Pausanias says he belonged to the second Messenian war and will discuss his exploits later.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Messenians gather at Stenyclerus after the capture of Amphea and prepare for war under Euphaes. They fight the Lacedæmonians, retreat to Ithome after suffering losses and pestilence, and continue the war with support from Arcadian allies.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Lacedæmonians raid Messenia, carry off cattle, grain, and fruit, and attack some towns without capturing them. They fight the Messenians in two major battles and later resume the war after hearing of the oracle.

l: Aristodemus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aristodemus, a member of the Æpytidæ, offers his daughter for the divinely required sacrifice. After killing her in anger over a false pregnancy claim, he is nevertheless elected king of the Messenians after Euphaes’s death.

l: Theopompus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Theopompus, son of Nicander and king of the Lacedæmonians, leads the right wing against the Messenians. He is routed by Euphaes in the first major battle and later fights Euphaes again in the second battle.

l: Euphaes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Euphaes urges the Messenians not to despair after Amphea falls and trains them for war. He leads them in battle, is mortally wounded while fighting Theopompus, survives briefly, and dies after ruling for thirteen years.

l: Amphea, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Amphea is captured by the Lacedæmonians before the events described in the main narrative. Its survivors report the capture to the Messenians, and its Lacedæmonian garrison later ambushes the returning envoy Tisis.

l: Messenia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Messenia is raided by the Lacedæmonians, who initially treat it as their own country and carry away its produce and livestock. The Messenians also raid the maritime parts of Laconia and farms near Mount Taygetus.

l: Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Messenians abandon their inland towns and settle at Ithome after their losses, desertions, and pestilence. They enlarge its small existing town because the mountain is a strong and difficult-to-access defensive position.

l: first Messenian battle, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: In the first major battle, Euphaes and the Messenians meet the Lacedæmonians at a place protected by a deep ravine. Euphaes’s men fortify their camp, while the fighting ends without a decisive victory and both sides later bury their dead.

l: second battle between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The second battle is fought after both Lacedæmonian kings lead an army against the Messenians. Euphaes’s division routs Theopompus’s troops, Pytharatus is killed on the Messenian side, and Euphaes is mortally wounded before the battle ends at nightfall.

l: capture of Amphea, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The capture of Amphea causes the Messenians to convene at Stenyclerus and begin urgent preparations for war. The event also leads to the enslavement or suffering of its inhabitants, as reported by those who escape.

l: Messenian oracle, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The oracle brought from Delphi commands the Messenians to sacrifice a pure virgin from the family of the Æpytidæ by night. If no suitable Æpytidæ could be found, the oracle allowed a willing volunteer from another family.

l: sacrifice of a pure virgin, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Æpytidæ draw lots, but the selected daughter of Lyciscus is rejected when Epebolus reveals that she is not truly Lyciscus’s daughter. Aristodemus then kills his own daughter after a false accusation of pregnancy, and Euphaes persuades the Messenians to regard her death as fulfilling the oracle.

l: warfare, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The warfare involves raids, fortified towns, heavy-armed infantry, cavalry, light-armed troops, and Cretan archers serving the Lacedæmonians. The combatants show intense courage, ask no quarter, and generally avoid pursuing fleeing enemies too far or breaking their formations.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: In the fifth year of Aristodemus’s reign, the Messenians and their Arcadian, Argive, and Sicyonian allies defeated the Lacedæmonians and Corinthians, after Aristodemus used light-armed troops to harass and surround the Spartan force. The Lacedæmonians and Messenians then consulted Delphi, whose ambiguous prophecies concerned guile, hidden things, and the tripods of Zeus of Ithome; Spartan stratagems failed, while Œbalus secretly placed clay tripods at the altar. Aristodemus later killed himself after ominous portents and the loss of hope, and the Messenians evacuated Ithome after twenty years of war, submitting to Spartan rule and tribute. Thirty-nine years later the Messenians rose again under Aristomenes, fought the battle of Deræ, and prepared to meet the Lacedæmonians and their allies at Boar’s Memorial.

l: Aristodemus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Aristodemus commanded the Messenian forces in the later stages of the first Messenian War, positioning the heavy-armed troops and concealing light-armed troops, slingers, and archers in Ithome. He later sent to Delphi, interpreted the omen concerning Ophioneus, and, believing that there was no hope of saving Messenia, cut his throat at his daughter’s grave after a reign of six years and a few months.

l: Tyrtæus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Tyrtæus’s verses were used to date the evacuation of Ithome and to describe the twenty years of the first Messenian War. During the second Messenian War, the Athenians sent him to Sparta in response to a Delphic oracle, and he recited elegiac verses and anapæsts to the Spartan authorities and people.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Aristomenes was among the young Messenian leaders who promoted a general rising against Spartan rule. After the undecided battle of Deræ, he was elected king and appointed commander in chief, and he later went by night to Sparta and hung a shield at the temple of Athene Chalciœcus, claiming it was taken from Spartan spoils.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Lacedæmonians suffered a major defeat in the battle described in Chapter XI and lost many excellent warriors. They unsuccessfully used supposed deserters and attempted to win over the Messenian allies, later captured Ithome, imposed tribute and other obligations on the Messenians, and fought the renewed Messenian rising in the second Messenian War.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Messenians and their allies defeated the Lacedæmonians after using light-armed troops to harass their flanks and disrupt their formation. After Aristodemus’s death they evacuated Ithome, were subjected to Spartan tribute and mourning requirements, and later rose in insurrection under Aristomenes with support from several allies.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Arcadians came to the aid of the Messenians in full force during the first Messenian War and fought alongside them. They rejected Spartan attempts to win them over, and during the second Messenian War they again supported the Messenians, including at the battle at Boar’s Memorial.

l: Messenia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Messenia was conquered by the Lacedæmonians after the evacuation and capture of Ithome. Its inhabitants were required to surrender half the produce of the land to Sparta and to mourn Spartan kings and officials, but the people later organized a general rising.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Sparta was the home of the Lacedæmonians and the place from which they sought Delphic advice and organized attempts to undermine the Messenians. Aristomenes entered Sparta by night and dedicated a shield at the temple of Athene Chalciœcus as a challenge to the Spartans.

l: Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Ithome served as the Messenian stronghold and was positioned behind the Messenian army during the battle in Chapter XI. After a siege lasting about five months at the end of the twenty-year first Messenian War, the Messenians evacuated it, and the Lacedæmonians subsequently razed it to the ground.

l: Delphi, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Delphi was consulted by both the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians about the war. Its priestess gave prophecies concerning cunning, hidden things, the tripods of Zeus of Ithome, and the future fortunes of the opposing sides.

l: Deræ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Deræ was a place in Messenia where the Messenians and Lacedæmonians fought during the first year of the second Messenian War. Neither side had allies, and the battle was undecided.

l: first Messenian War, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The first Messenian War ended after the Messenians had resisted for twenty years and evacuated Ithome. The Lacedæmonians then conquered the remaining Messenian cities and imposed tribute, oaths of submission, and compulsory mourning.

l: the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The second Messenian War began thirty-nine years after the capture of Ithome, in the fourth year of the 23rd Olympiad. The Messenians rose against Spartan rule, fought an undecided battle at Deræ, and prepared for a larger engagement with allies at Boar’s Memorial.

l: battle of Deræ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The battle of Deræ was fought in the first year of the second Messenian War without allies on either side. It ended without a decision, after which Aristomenes was elected king and appointed commander in chief by the Messenians.

l: battle at Boar’s Memorial, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The battle at Boar’s Memorial was prepared one year after the battle of Deræ, when both sides had assembled allies. The Messenians had support from Elis, Arcadia, Argos, Sicyon, the priests from Eleusis, and the descendants of Androcles, while the Lacedæmonians were supported by the Corinthians and some people of Lepreum; the Asinæi remained neutral.

l: capture and evacuation of Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Messenians evacuated Ithome after holding it for about five months under siege and after twenty full years of war. The Lacedæmonians then captured the other Messenian cities and first razed Ithome to the ground.

l: oracle at Delphi, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Pythian oracle told the Lacedæmonians that the Messenian land had been obtained by cunning and would be taken by the same means, but their attempted use of supposed deserters and efforts to corrupt allies failed. It later told the Messenians that the god granted them glory in war but warned them about treacherous Spartan ambushes, hidden things, fate, and the tripods of Zeus of Ithome.

l: tripods of Zeus of Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: A Delphic oracle promised the Messenian land to those who first set up one hundred tripods at the altar of Zeus of Ithome. The Messenians prepared wooden tripods, while Œbalus secretly placed one hundred clay tripods there for Sparta; the Messenians then placed their wooden tripods at the altar as well.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Aristomenes repeatedly defeats the Lacedæmonians, raids Laconia, survives capture in Ceadas, and continues leading the Messenian resistance from Eira. The Lacedæmonians bribe Aristocrates, whose betrayal causes the Messenians and Arcadians to lose the battle at the Great Trench, after which the Messenians retreat to Eira. Eira is besieged for eleven years, while Aristomenes conducts raids and resists the blockade. Theoclus interprets an oracle as foretelling the end of Messene, and Eira ultimately falls after a herdsman reveals that its defenses have been abandoned during a storm.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Aristomenes routs Anaxander's division and then defeats the wider Lacedæmonian force, though he loses his shield near a wild pear tree. He raids Pharis, escapes from Ceadas by following a fox, defeats Corinthian auxiliaries, and is later freed from Cretan bowmen by a young woman after being captured. During the siege of Eira he leads raids and rescues a Cephallenian merchant, but is wounded shortly before the guard abandons the citadel.

l: Theoclus the seer, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Theoclus serves as the Messenian seer and warns Aristomenes that Castor and Pollux are seated in the wild pear tree. After observing a fig tree touching the Neda, he interprets the oracle about a he-goat drinking from the river as a sign that Messene's safety has ended. He and Aristomenes had previously consulted Delphi after the disaster at the Great Trench.

l: Aristocrates, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Aristocrates, son of Icetas and king and general of the Arcadians, accepts a bribe from the Lacedæmonians. At the Great Trench he orders the Arcadians to flee, abandoning the Messenian centre and left wing and contributing to the Lacedæmonian victory. He completes his treason by fleeing through the Messenian lines.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Messenians fight the Lacedæmonians under Aristomenes and initially achieve victories, but suffer a major defeat at the Great Trench after Aristocrates withdraws the Arcadians. They retreat to Eira, raid Laconia and Messenia, and endure an eleven-year blockade. Their sacred records are hidden by Aristomenes on Mount Ithome so that they may retain hope of recovering their country.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Lacedæmonians fight Aristomenes and are repeatedly routed, but they recover after he loses his shield and later defeat the Messenians at the Great Trench by bribing Aristocrates. They besiege Eira, decree that Messenia and nearby parts of Laconia should not be cultivated, and use Corinthian forces and Cretan bowmen against the Messenians. Their siege ultimately benefits from a deserter's knowledge that the citadel guard has abandoned its posts.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Arcadians come from their cities to aid the Messenians at the Great Trench. Their king and general Aristocrates, after accepting Lacedæmonian money, orders them to flee at the start of the battle, leaving the Messenian centre and left wing exposed.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Sparta is threatened by Aristomenes, who intends to enter it by night and later raids nearby Amyclæ before help can arrive from Sparta. The city receives news of Aristomenes' actions and suffers scarcity and riots when cultivation is suspended during the war. The Lacedæmonians also return to Sparta to celebrate the festival of Hyacinthus.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Messene suffers defeat at the Great Trench and faces the loss of its territory during the siege of Eira. Theoclus interprets the Pythian oracle as declaring that its period of safety has ended. Aristomenes hides sacred records so that Messene may one day have a chance to recover its country.

l: Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Eira becomes the refuge of the Messenians after the defeat at the Great Trench and is besieged by the Lacedæmonians for eleven years. Its inhabitants raid enemy territory while defending the mountain stronghold, but its improvised fortifications lack battlements and turrets. During a violent rainstorm the guards abandon their posts, enabling a herdsman to reveal how the Lacedæmonians can capture it.

l: Laconia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Aristomenes raids Laconia, including Pharis, and carries off booty before defeating Lacedæmonian troops on the return journey. The Messenians later plunder Laconia from Eira, prompting the Lacedæmonians to prohibit cultivation in Messenia and neighboring parts of Laconia.

l: Ceadas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Ceadas is the underground cavern into which the Lacedæmonians throw their greatest malefactors. Aristomenes and captured Messenian soldiers are cast into it, but Aristomenes survives, follows a fox to an opening, enlarges the passage, and escapes.

l: siege of Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The siege of Eira lasts eleven years after the Messenian defeat at the Great Trench. During it, the Messenians conduct raids, while the Lacedæmonians attempt to take the stronghold and receive assistance from Corinthian troops and Cretan bowmen. The siege approaches its conclusion when a deserter informs Emperamus how the abandoned guard posts can be exploited.

l: fall of Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The fall of Eira is foretold by the oracle concerning the he-goat drinking from the Neda and is brought nearer when a herdsman learns that the Messenian guards have left their posts during heavy rain. The herdsman deserts to the Lacedæmonians and tells Emperamus how the stronghold can be captured.

l: first Messenian War, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The war features repeated battles between Aristomenes and the Lacedæmonians, including the defeat at the Great Trench and the prolonged resistance at Eira. Bribery, raids, sieges, omens, and divine assistance all shape its course, while Aristomenes preserves sacred records intended to support a future Messenian return.

l: Messenian resistance at Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Messenian resistance at Eira continues for eleven years after the disaster at the Great Trench. Aristomenes leads raids against Laconia and the Messenians ransom captives and property, while the defenders withstand the Lacedæmonian blockade. The resistance is undermined when a storm causes the guards to leave their posts and a herdsman betrays the stronghold's vulnerability.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Emperamus led the Spartans into Eira, whose capture ended the Messenian resistance after three days and nights of fighting. The surviving Messenians escaped under Aristomenes, while Theoclus died attacking the Lacedæmonians, and the Arcadians received the refugees at Mount Lycæus. Aristocrates betrayed Aristomenes’ plan to capture Sparta and was stoned to death. The exiled Messenians later settled in Sicily after Anaxilas helped them conquer Zancle and rename it Messene.

l: Emperamus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Emperamus led the Spartan force through the darkness and rain to Eira, where they entered the citadel by scaling its walls. He was pleased when Aristomenes signaled that the Messenians wished to withdraw, and he allowed them to pass through the lines.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aristomenes defended Eira, encouraged the Messenians during the fighting, and knew from the oracle about the he-goat and the wild fig tree that their cause was doomed. After Theoclus died, he organized the retreat of the Messenians, women, and children, led by Gorgus and Manticlus. At Mount Lycæus he planned to capture Sparta with 500 Messenians, but Aristocrates betrayed the plan.

l: Gorgus the son of Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Gorgus was among the first defenders to reach the fighting at Eira. Aristomenes appointed him, together with Manticlus, to lead the Messenians, women, and children during their retreat, and later he became one of the leaders of the Messenian settlement in Sicily.

l: Theoclus the seer, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Theoclus helped defend Eira and encouraged the Messenians by recalling the people of Smyrna’s resistance to Gyges and the Lydians. He told Aristomenes that Messene was destined to perish, then attacked the Lacedæmonians, killed several of them, and died from his wounds.

l: Manticlus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Manticlus fought among the first defenders of Eira and was appointed with Gorgus to lead the retreating Messenians. Later he argued that the exiles should sail to Sardinia, led the Messenian settlement in Sicily with Gorgus, and built a temple of Hercules for the new colony.

l: Emperamus and the Spartans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: They marched through darkness and heavy rain, entered Eira by scaling its walls, and fought the Messenians. They allowed Aristomenes and the retreating Messenians to pass through their lines rather than provoke men who were desperate and enraged.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Lacedæmonians captured Eira after prolonged fighting and incorporated the captured Messenians into the Helot population. Their forces used a rotation of fighting and resting to outlast the exhausted Messenians, and later plundered Messenian property.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aristomenes planned to attack and capture Sparta while most of the Lacedæmonians were at Eira or occupied with plundering. The plan failed after Aristocrates informed Anaxander at Sparta.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Messenians defended Eira for three days and nights despite rain, cold, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, with their women also taking up arms. After Eira fell, some were made Helots, while others escaped to Arcadia and later founded a settlement in Sicily.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Messene was the homeland the Messenians fought to preserve, but Theoclus and Aristomenes believed its destruction had been foretold. After Eira fell, the Messenians could no longer recover it, and the name was later given to the former Zancle in Sicily.

l: Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Eira was captured when Emperamus and the Spartan force entered its citadel by scaling the walls. Its fall ended the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians, and its captured inhabitants and property were dealt with by the Lacedæmonians.

l: the capture of Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The capture of Eira followed three days and nights of continuous fighting in severe rain and cold. It caused the fall of the last Messenian stronghold, the enslavement of many Messenians as Helots, and the flight of the remaining exiles.

l: the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The second war ended with the capture of Eira in the archonship of Autosthenes, in the first year of the 28th Olympiad, when Chionis the Laconian was victor.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Arcadians welcomed the surviving Messenians at Mount Lycæus, supplied them with food and clothing, and invited them to live in their cities. About 300 Arcadians wished to join Aristomenes’ planned attack on Sparta, while other Arcadians exposed Aristocrates’ betrayal and stoned him.

l: Aristocrates, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aristocrates refused to lead the Arcadians to aid the Messenians because he had been bribed by the Lacedæmonians. He twice betrayed the Messenians, first by abandoning them and later by sending Aristomenes’ plan to Anaxander, and the Arcadians stoned him to death and cast him outside their borders.

l: Mount Lycæus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Mount Lycæus was where the Arcadians met and welcomed the surviving Messenians after the fall of Eira. Aristomenes planned his attack on Sparta there, and Aristocrates’ betrayal was exposed before the Arcadians.

l: the 500 Messenian volunteers, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aristomenes selected 500 Messenians known to be willing to risk their lives and asked whether they would die with him to avenge their country. They agreed to his plan to attack Sparta, but the plan was revealed to the Lacedæmonians before it could be carried out.

l: the betrayal of Aristocrates, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aristocrates betrayed Aristomenes by sending Anaxander a letter revealing the planned attack on Sparta. The letter was intercepted by Arcadians, who showed Anaxander’s reply to the people and thereby exposed Aristocrates as a traitor.

l: Cyllene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Cyllene was the arsenal of Elis where the people of Pylos, Mothone, and other maritime towns took refuge after Eira fell. The exiled Messenians gathered there, wintered there with support from Elis, and considered where to establish a new home.

l: the Messenian colony, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Messenian colony was established in Sicily after the exiles accepted Anaxilas’ invitation and conquered Zancle. Its people changed the town’s name to Messene, and Manticlus built a temple of Hercules there.

l: Anaxilas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Anaxilas, king at Rhegium, invited the Messenian exiles to Italy and promised them the fertile territory and city of Zancle in Sicily. He helped them conquer the people of Zancle by blockading them from the sea while the Messenians attacked by land, and urged the Messenians to kill the suppliants and enslave the rest.

l: Rhegium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Rhegium was ruled by Anaxilas, who invited the Messenian exiles there before conveying them to Sicily. Anaxilas used the conflict between Rhegium and Zancle as the basis for the Messenians’ settlement.

l: Zancle, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Zancle had originally been occupied by pirates and served as a fortified base for expeditions by land and sea. Anaxilas and the Messenians conquered it, and its people took refuge at altars and temples before being spared and incorporated into the new community.

l: Sicily, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Sicily became the destination of the Messenian exiles after Anaxilas invited them to settle in Zancle. The Messenians conquered the city and established their new community there.

l: the people of Zancle, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The people of Zancle were defeated by Anaxilas at sea and by the Messenians on land. After their fort was taken, they sought refuge at altars and temples; Gorgus and Manticlus persuaded the others not to kill or enslave them, and they subsequently lived together as one people.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Aristomenes arranged marriages for his daughters, died before carrying out plans for vengeance against the Lacedæmonians, and was honored by Damagetus and the people of Rhodes. The Messenians who had become Helots revolted, established themselves at Ithome, later received Naupactus from the Athenians, and fought the Acarnanians at Œniadæ before escaping to Naupactus. After the victory at Leuctra, Epaminondas and the Thebans recalled the exiled Messenians, recovered the Messenian Mysteries, and restored Messene and other Messenian towns. The restored Messenians later resisted the Lacedæmonians, received aid from Philip and the Macedonians, and captured Elis by stratagem.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Aristomenes refused leadership of those going to the new colony, arranged marriages for his sister and daughters, and consulted the oracle at Delphi. He died of illness in Rhodes before he could travel to Sardis and Ecbatana to seek vengeance against the Lacedæmonians, and the Rhodians built a monument to him and honored his memory.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Lacedæmonians conquered and divided Messenia, excepting the territory of the Asinæi, and gave Mothone to the people of Nauplia. They later provoked the revolt of the Messenian Helots through the killing of suppliants at Tænarum, resisted the restoration of the Messenians, and eventually fought them again after the Thebans withdrew from the Peloponnese.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenians revolted from the Lacedæmonians, held out at Ithome, received Naupactus from the Athenians, and defeated the Acarnanians at Œniadæ before escaping the siege. After nearly 300 years away from the Peloponnese, they returned, rebuilt their country, preserved their customs and Doric dialect, resisted Sparta, received aid from Philip and the Macedonians, and captured Elis.

l: Helots, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenians captured at Eira were forcibly incorporated among the Helots. In the 79th Olympiad, the Messenian Helots revolted again from the Lacedæmonians and went to Mount Ithome.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Athenians sent troops to assist the Lacedæmonians against the rebels at Ithome, but the Lacedæmonians dismissed them because they suspected them of revolutionary ideas. The Athenians then became friendly with the Argives, gave Naupactus to the surrendering Messenians, and later assisted them with archers at Sphacteria; afterward they declined to join a Messenian incursion into Laconia but promised aid if the Lacedæmonians attacked Messenia.

l: Argives, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Argives became friendly with the Athenians after the Lacedæmonians dismissed the Athenian troops from Ithome. They later assisted the Messenians, chose Epiteles as their General and the restorer of Messene, and sacrificed to Argive Hera and Nemean Zeus during the restoration.

l: Acarnanians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Acarnanians were defeated by the Messenians at Œniadæ, then gathered forces from their towns and besieged the Messenians there. They maintained the blockade until the Messenians escaped, losing many men in the fighting.

l: Epaminondas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Epaminondas decided to restore the Messenians after the Theban victory at Leuctra and received a dream urging him to give them back their country and cities. He consulted Epiteles about the dream, directed the recovery of the Messenian Mysteries, selected the site for the new capital, and organized the building of Messene.

l: Epiteles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Epiteles, whom the Argives chose as their General and the restorer of Messene, was directed in a dream to dig between an ivy and myrtle tree at Ithome. He found a brass cinerary urn containing the written Mysteries of the Great Goddesses and took it to Epaminondas.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Messene, the daughter of Triopas, was invoked with other heroes to return and dwell with the restored Messenians. The priests and leaders called especially upon her during the sacrifices connected with the rebuilding of the Messenian capital.

l: Castor and Pollux, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Castor and Pollux were believed to have become hostile to the Messenians after Panormus and Gonippus profaned their festival by disguising themselves as the Twin Brethren and killing Lacedæmonians. Their wrath was later said to have been appeased, and the Messenians sacrificed to them during the restoration.

l: Thebans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: After the victory at Leuctra, the Thebans sent messengers to Italy, Sicily, and the Euesperitæ to recall the exiled Messenians. Epaminondas and the Thebans then helped establish the restored Messenian capital, and the Lacedæmonians refrained from interfering while the Thebans remained a threat.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Arcadians supplied victims for the sacrifices at the restoration of Messene and sacrificed to Dionysus and Apollo Ismenius. They also assisted the Messenians in their later war against the Lacedæmonians.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Elis, formerly regarded as orderly, fell into faction after influential people were corrupted by Philip, the son of Amyntas. About 1,000 Messenians entered Elis using Lacedæmonian colors on their shields, expelled the Lacedæmonian party, and entrusted the city to their own friends.

l: Messenia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Messenia was conquered and divided among the Lacedæmonians, while the Asinæi retained their territory and Mothone was given to the people of Nauplia. The Messenians were eventually restored to Messenia after nearly 300 years of exile.

l: Messene (city), Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The restored Messenians built Messene as a new capital after Epaminondas selected its site and received favorable omens. They constructed its walls, houses, streets, and temples, and also restored other Messenian towns.

l: Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Ithome became the stronghold of the revolting Messenian Helots. It was also the place where the recovered Messenian Mysteries were found, and Zeus of Ithome was honored during the restoration of Messene.

l: Eira, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Eira was captured by the Lacedæmonians, after which its Messenian inhabitants were incorporated among the Helots. Bacis was said to have foretold how Eira would be taken, and the Messenians returned to the Peloponnese 287 years after its capture.

l: Naupactus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Athenians gave Naupactus to the Messenians who surrendered at Ithome after taking it from the Locrians called Ozolæ. Naupactus became a Messenian base against the Peloponnese, and after its loss the Messenians dispersed to Sicily and Libya.

l: Œniadæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenians attacked Œniadæ, defeated its inhabitants, and occupied the town for about a year. The Acarnanians later besieged it, and the Messenians escaped by night after their supplies were exhausted, fighting their way through to Naupactus.

l: Peloponnese, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenians were allowed to evacuate the Peloponnese after the fall of Ithome. The Thebans later recalled them from exile, and they were restored to the Peloponnese 287 years after the capture of Eira.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Sparta was foretold by Bacis to lose its glorious flower when Messene was rebuilt. The Lacedæmonians of Sparta later resumed hostilities against the restored Messenians after the Phocian War drew the Thebans away from the Peloponnese.

l: Leuctra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Leuctra was the place of the Theban victory after which the long-fated disaster came upon the Lacedæmonians. The victory enabled the Thebans to recall the Messenians and support their restoration.

l: battle of Leuctra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Theban victory in the battle of Leuctra marked the reversal of Lacedæmonian fortune and led to the restoration of the Messenians. Afterward, Theban messengers summoned the exiled Messenians from Italy, Sicily, and the Euesperitæ.

l: the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Second Messenian revolt began when Messenian Helots rose against the Lacedæmonians after the killing of suppliants at Tænarum. The rebels went to Ithome, and the Lacedæmonians sought assistance from allies including Cimon and the Athenians.

l: Messenian return to the Peloponnese, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenian return to the Peloponnese followed the Theban victory at Leuctra and the recall issued by the Thebans. The exiles returned with strong attachment to their homeland and hatred of the Lacedæmonians, rebuilt Messene and other towns, and preserved their national customs and Doric dialect.

l: siege of Œniadæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: During the siege of Œniadæ, the Messenians initially defeated or repelled Acarnanian attacks but were eventually blockaded until their provisions ran out in the eighth month. They then escaped by night, losing about 300 men but killing more Acarnanians, and reached Naupactus with help from the Ætolians.

l: Messenian Mysteries, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Messenian Mysteries were recovered at Ithome when Epiteles found a brass urn containing their written records. The priests entered the records in books, and they sacrificed to the Great Goddesses and Caucon during the restoration of Messene.

l: restoration of Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The restoration of Messene was undertaken by Epaminondas, Epiteles, the Thebans, and their allies after the victory at Leuctra. The site was examined through omens, sacrifices were made to numerous gods and heroes, and the city’s walls, houses, streets, and temples were built while other Messenian towns were restored.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The unit recounts Demetrius, son of Philip, and the Macedonians' failed attempt to capture Messene, whose inhabitants repelled them with help from the citadel and the women of the town. It traces the Messenians' eventual entry into the Achæan League, their reception of the Arcadians after Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, and later conflicts involving Sparta, the Achæans, Philopœmen, and Dinocrates. It then describes Messenia, including Abia, Pharæ, Thuria, Messene, the Carnasian grove, and local temples, monuments, rivers, and traditions. The unit also records traditions about Aristomenes, Zeus at Ithome, and the shield of Aristomenes at the battle of Leuctra.

l: Demetrius, son of Philip, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Demetrius, son of Philip, led a Macedonian force sent by Philip to the Peloponnese in search of money. He landed in Argolis, marched secretly to Messene, entered the town before dawn, and was defeated when the Messenians and the citadel's garrison attacked him.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Messene repelled the Macedonian attack led by Demetrius, son of Philip. It later received the Arcadians who escaped from Megalopolis, granted them equal rights, resisted the Spartan tyrant Nabis, and eventually rejoined the Achæan League. The city is described as standing under Mount Ithome and surrounded by a strong stone wall with towers and battlements.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Macedonians under Demetrius, son of Philip, secretly entered Messene before dawn but were driven out by the Messenians and the citadel's garrison. Exhausted by their march, they fled in disorder, and many perished after being pushed from the precipitous rocks.

l: Peloponnese, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Peloponnese was the destination of Demetrius, son of Philip, when Philip sent him with a fleet to obtain money. The Messenians were restored there after having been scattered to distant places for a long time.

l: Ithome, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ithome was known to Demetrius, son of Philip, who used his knowledge of the road to enter Messene secretly. It was also the site of Messene's citadel, the spring Clepsydra, and the annual feast of Zeus of Ithome.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Lacedæmonians had friendly relations with the Messenians after the latter aided them against Pyrrhus. They were later opposed by the Achæans, defeated at Sellasia with Messenian participation, and ruled successively by Machanidas and Nabis after Cleomenes had been removed.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Messenians defeated Demetrius, son of Philip, after first mistaking his troops for Lacedæmonians. They eventually joined the Achæan League, sheltered the Arcadians who escaped from Megalopolis, helped take Sparta, resisted Nabis, and later captured Philopœmen before punishing those responsible for his death and rejoining the League.

l: Achæan league, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Messenians initially avoided the Achæan League because they did not wish to renew their feud with the Lacedæmonians. They later joined it, left it after a conflict with the Achæans, and rejoined it after those responsible for Philopœmen's death were punished.

l: Achæans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Achæans were openly hostile to the Lacedæmonians, partly because Argives and Arcadians were prominent among them. They fought alongside the Messenians at Sparta, later ravaged Messenia, and twice marched against the Messenians, though Dinocrates forced Lycortas and the Achæan army to withdraw.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Sparta was taken with the help of the Messenians, Aratus, and the Achæans after the battle against Cleomenes at Sellasia. It later faced the tyrants Machanidas and Nabis.

l: Cleomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Cleomenes, son of Leonidas and grandson of Cleonymus, captured Megalopolis during a truce. He was later defeated at Sellasia, where the Messenians joined Aratus and the Achæans in taking Sparta.

l: Megalopolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Megalopolis, the chief town of the Arcadians, was captured by Cleomenes during a truce. About one third of its inhabitants were captured or slain, while Philopœmen and more than two thirds of the people escaped and were received by the Messenians.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Arcadians had anciently shown friendliness toward the Messenians and had helped in rebuilding Messene. After Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, the escaping Arcadians were received by the Messenians, who granted them equal rights.

l: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, escaped from Megalopolis with the surviving Arcadians and was received by the Messenians. He later joined a night attack against Nabis, and during a later conflict with the Messenians he was captured alive and subsequently killed; the manner of his capture and death is deferred to the account of Arcadia.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Aristomenes was said by the Messenians to have fought for the Thebans at Leuctra and to have been a principal cause of the Lacedæmonian defeat. His shield, preserved at the temple of Trophonius, was displayed by the Thebans before the battle and returned there afterward; Messene also had his tomb and a bronze statue.

l: Dinocrates, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Dinocrates, a prominent Messenian recently elected ruler, forced Lycortas and the Achæan army to withdraw from Messenia without achieving their purpose. He then occupied the byroads between Messenia and Arcadia to protect the Messenians and their neighboring districts.

l: Abia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Abia was a town by the sea in Messenia, about 20 stades from the Chœrian dell. It was formerly called Ire, and tradition said that Abia, the nurse of Glenus, lived there, built a temple of Hercules, and gave the town its later name.

l: Pharæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Pharæ lay about 80 stades from Abia and about six stades from the sea. Its traditions included Pharis as founder, the healing powers of Nicomachus and Gorgasus, a temple and statue of Fortune, and the first known statue of Fortune by Bupalus.

l: Thuria, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Thuria, which was said to be Homer's Anthea, was given by Augustus to the Spartans. Its inhabitants moved from the ancient city on a height to the plain, where the river Aris flowed by the town, while ruins and a temple of the Syrian goddess remained above.

l: Clepsydra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Clepsydra was a well beneath Mount Ithome whose underground water fed the Arsinoe conduit in Messene. At the spring, the Messenians said, Ithome and Neda washed the infant Zeus after the Curetes had stolen him from Cronos.

l: Epaminondas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Epaminondas, son of Cleommis, had a statue in the temple of Æsculapius at Messene and an iron effigy made by another artist. The Thebans also honored Aristomenes before the battle of Leuctra, following the oracle of Trophonius, and Epaminondas persuaded Xenocrates to send for Aristomenes' shield.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Messenians said that Zeus was reared among them, with Ithome and Neda as his nurses. They worshipped Zeus of Ithome at a temple supplied with water from Clepsydra, kept his statue by an annually chosen priest, and celebrated an annual feast that originally included a musical contest.

l: Carnasian grove, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Carnasian grove stood opposite the plain of Stenyclerus at the site formerly called Œchalia. It contained statues of Carnean Apollo and Hermes, the statue of Demeter's daughter called the Virgin, and the sacred Mysteries of the Great Goddesses, which the narrator declined to reveal.

l: restoration of Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Messenians were described as having suffered dispersion to remote parts of the world before being restored to their own country long afterward. Their later history included renewed conflicts, refuge given to the Arcadians, participation in the capture of Sparta, the capture of Philopœmen, punishment of those responsible for his death, and renewed membership in the Achæan League.

l: capture of Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The attempted capture of Messene occurred when Demetrius, son of Philip, led Macedonian troops into the town before dawn. The inhabitants first mistook them for Lacedæmonians, then attacked them after recognizing their Macedonian arms and language; the Macedonians were defeated and many died among the rocks of Ithome.

l: battle of Leuctra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: At the battle of Leuctra, the Messenians said that Aristomenes fought for the Thebans and helped cause the Lacedæmonian defeat. The Thebans displayed Aristomenes' shield, following an oracle of Trophonius, and later returned it as a votive offering.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The unit describes the coast and inland places from Messene through Messenia, including the Pamisus, Corone, Asine, Mothone, Coryphasium, Pylos, and Cyparissiae. It records local traditions about temples, springs, founders, heroic figures, and the origins of the Dryopes and the people of Asine. It also recounts how Illyrian raiders deceived and captured many inhabitants of Mothone. The account ends by describing Pylos, its associations with Neleus and Nestor, the island of Sphacteria, and the Neda as the boundary between Messenia and Elis.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Messene is about 80 stades from the mouth of the Pamisus.

l: Pamisus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Pamisus flows clear and limpid through arable land and is navigable for about 10 stades inland. Sea fish, especially in spring, swim up it, and the fish are said to be finer in appearance because its water is clear rather than muddy. Corone lies on its right bank near the sea.

l: Corone, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Corone is a coastal town under Mount Mathia, about 80 stades from the Pamisus and about 40 stades from Colonides. It was formerly called Aepæ, and its name was later said to have been changed to Coronea and then mispronounced as Corone. It contains temples of Artemis, Dionysus, and Æsculapius, a statue of Zeus Soter in the market-place, and a statue of Athene holding a crow in the citadel.

l: Apollo, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: A temple of Apollo near the sea, about 80 stades from Corone, is held in high honour and is considered by the Messenians the most ancient of his temples. The god there is called Corydus and is believed to heal diseases. A wooden statue of him stands there, along with a brazen statue said to have been dedicated by the Argonauts.

l: Asine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Asine lies by the sea, about 40 stades from Colonides and about the same distance from the Promontory of Acritas. Its people, descendants of the Dryopes, say that they were defeated by Hercules, later settled in Asine in Argolis, and were eventually allowed by the Lacedæmonians to settle in Messenia. They retained their settlement after the restoration of the Messenians and celebrate annual mysteries of Dryops.

l: Dryopes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Dryopes were originally neighbours of the Lycoritæ near Mount Parnassus and were named after their founder. After their defeat by Hercules, different groups of their descendants settled in the Peloponnese and at Styra in Eubœa. The people of Asine proudly retain the name Dryopes and preserve temples and mysteries connected with Dryops.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Hercules defeated the Dryopes when Phylas was king and captured their town on Mount Parnassus. The people of Asine say that they fled after the capture and later crossed to the Peloponnese, where Eurystheus gave them Asine in Argolis.

l: Mothone, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Mothone was formerly called Pedasus and was said by its inhabitants to have taken its later name from Mothone, the daughter of Œneus. The account instead suggests that it was named after the Rock of Mothon, which forms a natural harbour and breakwater. Trajan granted the people of Mothone a free constitution, and the town contains temples of Athene and Artemis as well as a well whose water is mixed with pitch.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Lacedæmonians gave Mothone to the people of Nauplia after they had been expelled from their city for their Laconian sympathies. After the restoration of the Messenians, the Lacedæmonians did not prevent the people of Nauplia from remaining at Mothone.

l: Illyrians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Illyrians became masters of Epirus by a sudden attack and later equipped a fleet for piratic raids. At Mothone they pretended to trade peacefully, then captured many men and even more women and sailed away with them.

l: Coryphasium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The promontory of Coryphasium is about 100 stades from Mothone. Pylos lies near it.

l: Pylos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Pylos was founded by Pylos, the son of Cleson, who brought Leleges from Megaris, but he was expelled by Neleus and the Pelasgians of Iolcus. It contains a temple of Athene Coryphasia, a house called Nestor’s house, a painting of Nestor, Nestor’s tomb, and a cave said to have been the stall of the oxen of Nestor and earlier of Neleus. The district is mostly sandy and is associated with the epithet “sandy Pylos.”

l: Neleus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Neleus and the Pelasgians of Iolcus expelled Pylos, the son of Cleson, from Pylos. Neleus later advanced Pylos to such renown that Homer called it the city of Neleus. He was said to have possessed oxen descended from the herd of Iphiclus.

l: Nestor, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Pylos contains a house called Nestor’s house, a painting of Nestor, and his tomb inside the city. A cave there is said to have been the stall of Nestor’s oxen and, earlier, of Neleus’s oxen.

l: Sphacteria, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Sphacteria lies before the harbour of Pylos, much as Rhenea lies in relation to the harbour of Delos. The reverses of the Lacedæmonians there made the island world-famous, and the Athenians erected a brazen statue of Victory in their Acropolis to commemorate their success.

l: Mothone's capture by the Illyrians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Illyrians first anchored at Mothone as if they intended friendly commerce and gradually encouraged the inhabitants to come aboard their ships. When the traffic had grown, they seized many men and more women, put them on board, and sailed away toward the Ionian sea, leaving the town partly stripped of its population.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The unit recounts the origins, royal succession, colonization, and political history of Elis, including its connections with Ætolia, Arcadia, Achaia, and the Dorians. It describes conflicts involving Augeas, Hercules, Phyleus, Pisa, Pylos, Argives, and Corinth, as well as the traditions surrounding the Isthmian and Olympian games. Oxylus led the Dorian return to the Peloponnese and established a mixed Epean and Ætolian population in Elis. The account ends with Iphitus’s revival of the Olympian games and Elis’s later alliances and wars with the Lacedæmonians, Macedonians, and other Greek peoples.

l: Peloponnese, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Peloponnese is described as divided into five parts, including Arcadia, Achaia, and three Dorian regions. Arcadians and Achæans are identified as indigenous peoples, while other inhabitants came from elsewhere.

l: Arcadia, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Arcadia is one of the divisions of the Peloponnese and has always been inhabited by Arcadians. The Dorians later passed through Arcadia during their return to the Peloponnese.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Arcadians are identified as an indigenous people of the Peloponnese who remained in Arcadia. They assisted the people of Elis during Hercules’s campaign against Augeas, and later some joined conflicts involving Elis.

l: Achaia, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Achaia is identified as the second division of the Peloponnese. It was formerly called Ægialus, where the Ionians lived before the Achæans displaced them.

l: Achæans, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Achæans are described as indigenous to the Peloponnese but were driven from their original land by the Dorians. They displaced the Ionians in Ægialus, later called Achaia, and some Achæans colonized Elis with Agorius.

l: Dorians, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Dorians came from Mount Œta and displaced the Achæans from their original land. Under the sons of Aristomachus, they sought to return to the Peloponnese and accepted Oxylus as their leader.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Elis was originally settled by people from Calydon and other parts of Ætolia, and its inhabitants were successively called Epeans and Eleans. Its history includes wars with Hercules, disputes with Pisa and the Arcadians over Olympia, the settlement of Oxylus, and the revival of the Olympian games by Iphitus.

l: Ætolia, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Ætolia was named after Ætolus, who fled there from the Peloponnese after unintentionally killing Apis. Oxylus later left Ætolia after accidentally killing his brother and introduced Ætolians as colonists into Elis.

l: Epeus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Epeus won the footrace held by Endymion at Olympia and became king, after which his people were first called Epeans. He married Anaxiroe and had a daughter, Hyrmina, but no male heir.

l: Ætolus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Ætolus succeeded Epeus but fled the Peloponnese after accidentally killing Apis during funeral games. He went to the region near the Achelous River, which was subsequently called Ætolia after him.

l: Pelops, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Pelops came from Asia Minor, deposed Œnomaus, occupied Pisæa and Olympia, and took territory bordering Pisæa from Epeus. The people of Elis credited him with building the first temple to Hermes in the Peloponnese and sacrificing to the god for the murder of Myrtilus.

l: Eleus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Eleus, the son of Eurycyde and allegedly Poseidon, ruled the kingdom of the Epeans. During his reign, his people changed their name from Epeans to Eleans.

l: Eleans, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Eleans were formerly called Epeans and took their later name during the reign of Eleus. They fought Hercules with assistance from Pylos and Pisa, and later participated in conflicts involving the Dorians, Persians, Lacedæmonians, Macedonians, and other Greeks.

l: Augeas, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Augeas ruled Elis and possessed such numerous oxen and goats that their dung hindered cultivation. He hired Hercules to clear it, refused to pay the promised reward, expelled his son Phyleus for defending Hercules, and prepared for war; Hercules eventually captured Elis, forgave Augeas, and restored Phyleus.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Hercules cleared Augeas’s land by diverting the river Menius but was denied his reward. He later defeated Augeas, captured and sacked Elis, killed the sons of Actor at Cleonæ, and persuaded the Eleans to sacrifice to him after they had regarded him as hostile.

l: Phyleus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Phyleus, the eldest son of Augeas, was expelled for saying that Augeas should reward Hercules justly. Hercules later gave him Elis and other places, along with the captives, and Phyleus returned to Dulichium after settling affairs in Elis.

l: Argives, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Argives refused to surrender Hercules when the people of Elis demanded compensation for the killing of the sons of Actor. They later assisted Hercules in his campaign against Elis and subsequently allied with the Mantineans and Athenians against the Lacedæmonians.

l: Corinth, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Corinth is associated with the Isthmian games and with a tradition explaining the exclusion of the people of Elis from them. Corinthians also announced a truce during the Isthmian games, allowing the sons of Actor to attend before Hercules killed them.

l: Isthmian games, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Isthmian games were the occasion of a truce during which the sons of Actor left to attend and were ambushed by Hercules. The people of Elis traditionally abstained from the games because of curses attributed to Moline, although the text gives competing explanations for this practice.

l: Pylos, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The men of Pylos in Elis assisted the people of Elis and Pisa against Hercules. Hercules later punished the men of Pylos.

l: Pisa, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Pisa assisted Elis during Hercules’s campaign against Augeas. Hercules intended to attack Pisa but was stopped by an oracle from Delphi, and Elis later had frequent disputes with Pisa over the restoration of the games at Olympia.

l: Delphi, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Delphi issued an oracle that prevented Hercules from marching against Pisa. Its priestess later instructed Iphitus to join the people of Elis in restoring the Olympian games.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Olympia was the site where Endymion made his sons compete for the kingdom and where Pelops later established control. It was also the center of the contests whose restoration caused disputes between Elis, Pisa, and the Arcadians.

l: Dorians' return to the Peloponnese, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: During the Dorians’ planned return to the Peloponnese, an oracle instructed them to choose a three-eyed man as leader. They accepted Oxylus, followed his advice to travel by ship, and agreed to give him the kingdom of Elis.

l: Oxylus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Oxylus, an Ætolian who had fled after accidentally killing his brother, led the Dorians to the Peloponnese and received the kingdom of Elis. He defeated Elis’s champion through a single combat, allowed the Epeans to remain, introduced Ætolian colonists, consolidated the population of Elis, and invited Agorius and other Achæans to settle there.

l: Iphitus, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Iphitus, a relative of Oxylus and a contemporary of Lycurgus, revived the contest at Olympia and established a truce for its duration. At Delphi’s direction, he joined the people of Elis in restoring the Olympian games and persuaded them to sacrifice to Hercules.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Olympian games had been discontinued before Iphitus’s time. Iphitus restored them with the people of Elis after receiving instructions from the priestess at Delphi.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Lacedæmonians joined Elis, reluctantly, in invading Attica, but later fought Elis after Elis allied with the Mantineans, Argives, and Athenians. They were defeated by Elis at Olympia during an incursion under Agis, and Elis later joined Philip in attacking them because of their ancient hostility.

l: Laconia, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Lacedæmon is associated with Lycurgus, whose legislation was contemporary with Iphitus. The unit also refers to a later war between Elis and the Lacedæmonians, whose settlement had been described earlier.

l: Philip, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Philip, the son of Amyntas, sought to dominate Greece. The people of Elis, weakened by internal factions, joined the Macedonians but did not fight against the Greeks at Chæronea; they did participate in Philip’s attack on the Lacedæmonians.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The Macedonians received the support of Elis after Philip’s intervention in Greece. After Alexander’s death, the people of Elis joined the Greeks in fighting against Antipater and the Macedonians.

l: Olympic truce, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: Iphitus established a truce that lasted as long as the games at Olympia continued. The truce formed part of his restoration of the Olympian games.

l: oracle at Delphi, Description of Greece, BOOK V.--ELIS.
s: The oracle of Delphi told the Dorians to make a man with three eyes their leader, which led them to accept Oxylus. It also directed Iphitus to join the people of Elis in restoring the Olympian games, and an earlier oracle protected Pisa from Hercules’s attack.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Aristotimus briefly rules Elis before Chilon, Hellanicus, Lampis, and Cylon depose and kill him. The account describes Elis and Triphylia, including the flax of Elis, Lepreus, the rivers Aniger and Acidas, and the cave of the Nymphs of the Aniger. It also recounts Scillus, Xenophon’s residence there, and the punishment associated with Mount Typæum for women entering the Olympian contests. At Olympia, Pausanias describes the Alpheus and traditions concerning the origins and early history of the Olympian Games.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Elis was ruled by Aristotimus, son of Damaretus and grandson of Etymon, with assistance from Antigonus, but Aristotimus was deposed and killed after six months by Chilon, Hellanicus, Lampis, and Cylon. Elis was known for flax that grew there and nowhere else in Greece, and for the supposed curse preventing mares from bearing foals to he-asses within its borders. The people of Elis fought wars including the conflict with Pisa and later claimed to have recovered Scillus.

l: Samicum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Samicum was a coastal place near the district of Triphylia and the city of Lepreus. A road from Samicum led to Lepreus beside the river Aniger, and the river had its outlet to the sea after passing through Samicum. Samia, a town above Samicum, was said to have been made into an offensive fortress against the Arcadians by Polysperchon.

l: Lepreus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Lepreus was a city in Triphylia whose people claimed to belong properly to Arcadia, though they had long been subject to Elis. Its name was variously attributed to Lepreus, son of Pyrgeus; Leprea, daughter of Pyrgeus; or the leprosy of its early inhabitants. In Pausanias’s time it contained a temple of Demeter but no remarkable tomb or other temple, although its people remembered former shrines and tombs.

l: Aniger, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The Aniger flowed into the sea near Samicum, and its flow was often blocked by sand driven inland by violent winds. It rose in the Arcadian mountain Lapithus and had an unpleasant smell; before receiving the Acidas it contained no fish, and afterward its fish were inedible. Traditions attributed its smell to wounds washed in it by Chiron or Pylenor, to Hydra poison, or to the purifications of the daughters of Prœtus. A cave of the Nymphs of the Aniger stood nearby, where sufferers from leprosy prayed, sacrificed, and bathed in the river in the hope of being cured.

l: Scillus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Scillus was a town of Triphylia that allied itself with Pisa in the war against Elis, after which the people of Elis dispossessed its inhabitants. The Lacedæmonians later took Scillus from Elis and gave it to Xenophon. The district had wild animals suitable for hunting and was crossed by the river Selinus.

l: Xenophon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Xenophon, son of Gryllus, was exiled from Athens for joining Cyrus against the Persian king. The Lacedæmonians gave him Scillus, where he lived and built a temple and grove to Ephesian Artemis. The people of Elis said he was tried before the Olympian council for accepting Scillus but was acquitted, and they showed a tomb with an effigy said to represent him.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Olympia lay beyond Scillus across the Alpheus and was associated with the Olympian Games and contests. Its traditions included the temple of Cronos, the early races of the Idæan Dactyli, and contests involving Zeus, Cronos, Apollo, Hermes, and Ares. Near Olympia, Mount Typæum was used as the place from which women detected entering forbidden contests were to be thrown.

l: Alpheus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The Alpheus was a large and pleasant river whose source was in Arcadia rather than Elis. It received seven notable tributaries, including the Helisson, Brentheates, Gortynius, Buphagus, Ladon, Erymanthus, and the Cladeus. Traditions said that Alpheus was once a hunter who loved Arethusa and that the river flowed under the sea to join the spring at Ortygia, near Syracuse.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: According to the ancient archives of Elis, Cronos was the first king of Heaven and had a temple built to him at Olympia. Idæan Hercules was said to have instituted the Olympian Games after racing his four brothers and to have set their interval at every fifth year because the brothers were five. Other traditions connected the Games with contests between Zeus and Cronos or with Zeus’s victory over Cronos.

l: Olympian contests, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Women of Elis who competed in the Olympian contests or crossed the Alpheus on forbidden days were traditionally to be hurled from Mount Typæum. Callipatira, also called Pherenice by some, was the only woman said to have been detected; she had disguised herself as an athlete to bring her son to Olympia. She was spared because of her family’s victories, but a law was then made requiring athletes to compete naked.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The unit recounts the origins, development, additions, and discontinuations of contests at Olympia, naming figures such as Clymenus, Endymion, Pelops, Hercules, Iphitus, and numerous victors. It explains changes to the Olympic programme, the scheduling of events, and the number and organization of the umpires of the games. It also describes the Altis, the temple and statue of Zeus at Olympia, their dedications and sculptures, and the artists associated with them. The temple’s decoration includes the chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus, the fight between the Lapithæ and Centaurs, and many of the Labours of Hercules.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Olympia is described as the site where Clymenus established games and erected an altar to Hercules and the other Curetes. Its contests were later renewed by Iphitus and gradually expanded to include running, wrestling, boxing, horse-races, the pentathlum, and the pancratium.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Hercules is associated with the early games at Olympia, where Clymenus erected an altar to him and gave him the title of Assistant. Hercules is said to have won wrestling and the pancratium, and the temple at Olympia displays many of his Labours.

l: Pelops, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Pelops made the contest to Olympian Zeus more famous than his predecessors. The temple at Olympia represents his chariot race against Œnomaus, and also depicts Pelops with Hippodamia, his charioteer, horses, and grooms.

l: Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Games at Olympia were held in honor of Olympian Zeus. The temple and statue dedicated to Zeus were built from spoils taken after the people of Elis destroyed Pisa.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Elis controlled the games and repeatedly altered their programme, instituting some contests and discontinuing others. Its people are said to have disliked the horse, and they later organized the umpires of the games according to the number of tribes in Elis.

l: Iphitus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Iphitus renewed the Olympian games after their suspension following the reign of Oxylus. He was originally the sole umpire, and the posterity of Oxylus succeeded him in that role.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Olympic games were said to have been established or renewed by several early figures, including Clymenus, Endymion, Pelops, Amythaon, Pelias, Neleus, Augeas, Hercules, and Iphitus. After their revival, contests were added over time, including the double course, pentathlum, wrestling, boxing, horse-races, the pancratium, boys’ events, the race in heavy armour, and races for colts.

l: pentathlum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The pentathlum was remembered and added to the games in the 18th Olympiad, when Lampis was victorious. A pentathlum for boys was established in the 38th Olympiad but was discontinued after Eutelidas of Lacedæmon won it, because Elis did not wish its boys to train for the event.

l: pancratium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The pancratium was introduced at Olympia in the eighth Olympiad after the 25th, when Lygdamis of Syracuse defeated the competitors. A pancratium for boys was added in the 145th Olympiad, and Phædimus of the Troad won it.

l: Umpires of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The games originally had Iphitus as their sole umpire, followed by the posterity of Oxylus. The number later increased from two to nine, then ten, twelve, eight, and finally ten again as the organization and tribal divisions of Elis changed.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The sacred grove of Zeus at Olympia was called Altis, a slightly altered form of the Greek word for grove. Pindar also used the name Altis in an ode composed for a victor at Olympia.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The temple at Olympia was dedicated to Zeus and contained his statue. Its decoration included a golden Victory in the middle of the gable, a golden shield bearing the Gorgon Medusa, and other votive offerings.

l: Temple of Zeus at Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The temple of Zeus at Olympia was a Doric stone building designed by Libon of Elis, measuring 68 feet high to the gable, 95 feet wide, and 230 feet long. Its roof was made of Pentelican marble tiles, and its gables displayed the chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus and the fight between the Lapithæ and Centaurs.

l: statue of Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The statue of Zeus at Olympia was made by Phidias, as shown by the inscription naming Phidias the Athenian, son of Charmides. The statue stood in the temple whose gables and surrounding decorations included numerous mythological scenes.

l: Phidias, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Phidias of Athens, son of Charmides, is identified by an inscription as the maker of the statue of Zeus at Olympia. Alcamenes is described as his contemporary and second only to him as a statuary.

l: chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus was represented in bas relief on one of the temple’s gables at Olympia. The scene showed both chariots in motion, with Zeus in the center and the associated figures, horses, and rivers arranged on either side.

l: Œnomaus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Œnomaus appears on the temple gable at Olympia wearing a helmet and standing beside his wife Sterope. His charioteer Myrtilus and two unnamed grooms are also depicted with his chariot and four horses.

l: Labours of Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VIII.
