s: Most of the Labours of Hercules were represented in relief at Olympia. They included the hunting of the Erymanthian boar, taking the mares of Diomede, stealing the oxen of Geryon, supporting Atlas’s load, clearing Elis of its dung, taking the Amazon’s belt, and encounters involving the stag, Minotaur, Stymphalian birds, hydra, and Nemean lion.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit describes the gold-and-ivory statue of Olympian Zeus at Olympia, including its throne, paintings, ornaments, and the traditions surrounding its creation and preservation. It records the offerings and monuments in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, along with the grove of Pelops, the great altar, and numerous other altars. It explains Elis's sacrificial customs, including the use of white poplar wood, the role of the Alpheus, and restrictions connected with sacrifices to Pelops. It also recounts traditions about Hercules, Pelops, the Olympic contests, and the protective or prophetic significance of various rites and objects.

l: Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Olympian Zeus is worshipped at Olympia through a great gold-and-ivory statue, sacrifices, votive offerings, and a major altar. The people of Elis sacrifice to him at several altars, including the temple altar, the great altar made from sacrificial debris, and altars associated with cleansing, lightning, and other aspects of Zeus.

l: Phidias, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Phidias made the gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus and decorated its throne with figures and scenes. He represented the three Graces and three Seasons above Zeus's head, and tradition says that Zeus answered Phidias's prayer about the finished work by striking the pavement with lightning.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Hercules appears in the paintings on the panels around Zeus's throne, including scenes in which he bears the burden of Atlas, fights the Nemean lion, releases Prometheus, and fights the Amazons. Hercules is also said to have dedicated the grove of Pelops, sacrificed to Zeus at Olympia, introduced the white poplar from Thesprotia, and driven flies from the sacrifices by worshipping Zeus the Averter of Flies.

l: Zeus statue, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The statue is seated on a throne and wears a gold robe, sandals, and an olive-leaf crown; it holds a Victory in its right hand and a jewelled sceptre with an eagle in its left. Its ivory is protected at Olympia with oil because of the dampness of the grove, while water is used for Athena's ivory statue at Athens; the statue at Epidaurus needs neither because it and its throne stand over a well.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Olympia contains the Temple of Zeus, the grove of Pelops, the great altar, numerous other altars, monuments, paintings, and votive offerings. Its rituals include sacrifices by the people of Elis, the use of white poplar wood, and observances connected with the Olympic contests.

l: Temple of Zeus at Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Temple of Zeus at Olympia houses the gold-and-ivory statue, a woollen purple veil, votive offerings, imperial statues, crowns, shields, pillars, and other dedications. Its ante-chapel contains the horses of Cynisca, while one pillar records a hundred-year alliance between Elis, Athens, Argos, and Mantinea.

l: throne of Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The throne is richly adorned with gold, precious stones, ebony, ivory, painted animals, and worked figures. It has four feet, supporting pillars, Victories, scenes of contests and mythic battles, and panels painted by Panænus; the panels include Atlas, Hercules, Theseus and Pirithous, Salamis, Prometheus, Penthesilea, Achilles, and the Hesperides.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Elis preserves the rites and traditions of Olympia, including sacrifices to Zeus, Pelops, and many other deities. Its people use only white poplar wood for sacrifices to Zeus, maintain the great altar, and are said to have received the recovered bone of Pelops and made its finder Damarmenus and his descendants custodians.

l: Pelops, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Pelops is honoured at Olympia nearly as highly among heroes as Zeus is among gods. A tradition says that a shoulder-blade of Pelops was brought to Troy, later recovered from the sea near Euboea, and given to Elis, but it had disappeared by the time of the account.

l: enclosure sacred to Pelops, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The grove of Pelops lies north of the Temple of Zeus and extends from the middle of the temple toward its rear. It is enclosed by a stone wall, planted with trees, filled with statues and offerings, and entered from the west; sacrifices there include a black ram, whose flesh imposes restrictions on entry to the Temple of Zeus.

l: Alpheus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Alpheus is used by the seers of Olympia when they knead sacrificial debris to renew the great altar on the nineteenth day of Elaphius. It is regarded as especially friendly to Olympian Zeus, and altars at Olympia are dedicated jointly to Alpheus and Artemis and separately to Alpheus.

l: altar of Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The altar of Olympian Zeus is made from the debris of the thigh bones of sacrificed victims and stands between the grove of Pelops and the Temple of Hera. It has a lower pro-altar and a higher altar, with steps to the former and debris steps to the latter; victims are sacrificed below, while their thigh bones are burned above.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Olympic festival is associated with contests for boys and other ancient competitions represented on the throne of Zeus. The account also mentions the victory of Pantarces in boys' wrestling at the 86th Olympiad and the memorial horses of Cynisca for her victory at Olympia.

l: Olympian altar ritual, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The altar ritual at Olympia includes sacrifices in a prescribed sequence, beginning with Vesta and continuing with Olympian Zeus, Hermes, Artemis, Athena, Alpheus, and other deities. At the great altar, victims are sacrificed at the lower level and their thigh bones are burned at the top; seers annually renew the altar with debris mixed with water from the Alpheus.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The unit describes the altars, buildings, rituals, and priestly offices within and around Altis at Olympia, including the Town Hall of the people of Elis and the continuing fire on its hearth. It recounts the temple of Hera, the Hera Festival, the sixteen matrons who administer it, and the maiden races held there. It also describes the statues and mythological scenes in Hera’s temple, especially the chest of Cypselus, which depicts episodes involving Pelops, Hercules, and other heroes.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Altis contains numerous altars, including those of Aphrodite, the Seasons, Artemis, Zeus, Apollo, Dionysus, the Fates, Hermes, Poseidon, Hera, Castor and Pollux, Ares, Athene, Pan, and Aphrodite. It also contains the Town Hall of the people of Elis and is entered by a road used for processions.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Olympia has the workshop of Phidias outside Altis and the temple of Hera within the sanctuary. Its victors receive crowns made from the wild olive tree growing behind the temple.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Elis has a Town Hall within Altis, where sacrifices, hymns, and banquets for victors at Olympia are conducted. Its people consult the oracle at Libya and honor Greek, Libyan, and heroic figures.

l: Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Dionysus has an altar in front of the Seat of Honour at Olympia. He was also said to have been first worshipped by Narcæus and Physcoa.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Zeus is honored at Olympia by altars including those of Zeus of the Market-Place, Zeus Supreme, and the Decider of Fate. The Decider of Fate is explained as a title of Zeus because he fore-knows human events, including what the Fates send.
